It decides among store_by_pieces, set_storage_via_setmem, and related fallback paths based on size, alignment, and value form. final_method_items.reason: Most likely fix point. The bug is fundamentally a bad strategy choice for inline constant-size memset on x86: GCC chooses a scalar integer algorithm even though SSE unaligned vector stores are clearly legal and profitable for this exact 64-byte case. This function explicitly selects the stringop algorithm based on size, speed, and target costs, so it is the strongest candidate for steering memset toward an SSE-capable expansion path.

The observed output of eight movq stores matches a piece-size/mode-selection issue here. If the fix is to allow/promote V16QI/TImode style stores for fixed-size fills with runtime byte values, this is a direct implementation point.

final_method_items.summary: Expand string move (memcpy) ot store (memset) operation. Use i386 string operations when profitable. The code depends upon architecture, block size and alignment, but always has one of the following overall structures: Aligned move sequence: 1) Prologue guard: Conditional that jumps up to epilogues for small blocks that can be handled by epilogue alone. This is faster but also needed for correctness, since prologue assume the block is larger than the desired alignment. Optional dynamic check for size and libcall for large blocks is emitted here too, with -minline-stringops-dynamically. 2) Prologue: copy first few bytes in order to get destination aligned to DESIRED_ALIGN. It is emitted only when ALIGN is less than DESIRED_ALIGN and up to DESIRED_ALIGN - ALIGN bytes can be copied. We emit either a jump tree on power of two sized blocks, or a byte loop. 3) Main body: the copying loop itself, copying in SIZE_NEEDED chunks with specified algorithm. 4) Epilogue: code copying tail of the block that is too small to be handled by main body (or up to size guarded by prologue guard). Misaligned move sequence 1) missaligned move prologue/epilogue containing: a) Prologue handling small memory
final_method_items.reason: Central x86 string/memory expansion routine that decides algorithm, alignment handling, and profitability for memset lowering. Because the bug is x86-specific code-quality for inline constant-size memset under SSE4.2, this is one of the strongest backend-level fix locations.

behavior_items: The reproducer compares two semantically equivalent ways to fill 64 bytes of memory with the same byte value under `-O3 -msse4.2`: an explicit SIMD-style implementation (`Test`) and a library-style bulk fill (`TestStd` using `memset`).

In `Test`, the byte source is `dst[-1]`, so the function first loads the byte immediately preceding the destination pointer. `movzbl -1(%rdi), %eax` zero-extends that byte into a general-purpose register.

`_mm_set1_epi8(dst[-1])` conceptually broadcasts one 8-bit value into all 16 lanes of an `__m128i`. GCC materializes this with `movd %eax, %xmm0` and `pshufb %xmm1, %xmm0`, after zeroing `%xmm1` via `pxor %xmm1, %xmm1`. This produces a 128-bit vector whose every byte equals the loaded value.
The loop `for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` has a constant trip count and fixed 16-byte stride, so at `-O3` GCC fully unrolls it into four independent stores.

Each unrolled iteration stores the same 16-byte SIMD pattern to `dst + 16*i`, emitted as `movups %xmm0, offset(%rdi)` for offsets 0, 16, 32, and 48. The result is a 64-byte fill performed with four 128-bit SSE stores.

Although the source code in `Test` shows `_mm_loadu_si128(reinterpret_cast<__m128i*>(dst + 16 * i), pattern);`, the behavior being exercised is clearly that of an unaligned 128-bit store intrinsic such as `_mm_storeu_si128`; the shown assembly confirms stores, not loads. The reproducer is therefore about code generation strategy, not intrinsic correctness.
`TestStd` expresses the same final memory effect more abstractly: `memset(s, s[-1], 64)` fills exactly 64 bytes at `s` with the byte value read from the preceding location.
Because the fill size 64 is a compile-time constant, GCC does not emit a call to the runtime `memset`; instead it expands the operation inline.

The inlined expansion for `TestStd` stays in integer registers rather than using SSE registers, despite SSE4.2 being enabled. GCC loads the byte with `movzbl -1(%rdi), %eax` and then constructs a repeated-byte 64-bit pattern using the constant `0x0101010101010101` (`72340172838076673`).

The integer sequence `imulq`, `mulq`, and `addq` is used to replicate the 8-bit value across 64 bits. Once GCC has two 64-bit pieces available in `%rax` and `%rdx`, it emits eight 8-byte stores to cover the 64-byte destination region.

The resulting `TestStd` code performs stores at offsets 0, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, and 56 using `movq`, so the same 64-byte memory effect is achieved through scalar integer stores rather than four vector stores.

The bug report is specifically highlighting a code-generation quality issue: for a constant-size `memset` of 64 bytes on a target with SSE4.2, GCC chooses a scalarized integer expansion instead of a vectorized SSE expansion similar to the one produced for the hand-written intrinsic version.

The reproducer therefore exercises GCC's optimization pipeline in two different forms: direct vector IR induced by intrinsics versus built-in/libcall expansion of `memset`. The former reaches an SSE-friendly lowering path, while the latter appears to go through a generic constant-size memset expander that prefers integer replication and scalar stores.

This is not a functional miscompilation in the shown example: both functions write the same 64-byte pattern derived from the preceding byte. The observable issue is the discrepancy in generated machine code and likely performance characteristics.

A key compiler-behavior point is that GCC recognizes and aggressively optimizes both forms, but its cost model or expander for constant-size `memset` does not exploit available SIMD instructions here, even though the architecture and optimization level would make that a plausible choice.

The reproducer is minimal because it isolates only three ingredients: a nonconstant fill byte loaded from memory, a fixed fill length of 64 bytes, and x86-64 with SSE4.2 enabled. That makes the difference in lowering strategy easy to attribute to GCC's `memset` expansion decisions rather than to aliasing, control flow, or unknown alignment.

The generated `movups` in `Test` also shows GCC intentionally uses unaligned vector stores, matching the semantics of an unaligned destination pointer. Therefore lack of proven alignment is not, by itself, a reason GCC could not have used SSE stores for the `memset` case as well.

Overall, the reproducer demonstrates that hand-written SIMD intrinsics lead GCC to emit four 16-byte stores, while equivalent source written as `memset(..., ..., 64)` is expanded into scalar byte-broadcast arithmetic plus eight 8-byte stores, exposing the optimization gap reported in bug 101366.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer shows a GCC code-generation mismatch for two equivalent 64-byte fill operations on x86-64 with `-O3 -msse4.2`. The intrinsic-based version explicitly creates a 16-byte vector filled with `dst[-1]` and is optimized into four unaligned SSE stores (`movups`). The `memset(s, s[-1], 64)` version is also inlined, but GCC expands it through an integer constant-size memset path: it broadcasts the byte using multiplication by `0x0101010101010101` and emits eight 64-bit scalar stores. Both are functionally correct, but the reproducer exposes that GCC's constant-size `memset` lowering does not use SSE instructions here even though vector code is available and naturally generated for the equivalent hand-written SIMD form.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is a constant-size bulk memory fill of 64 bytes with a runtime byte value loaded from memory, on x86-64 with SSE4.2 enabled. Two semantically equivalent forms are presented: one written with explicit SIMD operations and one written as memset. GCC lowers the explicit SIMD form into a broadcast plus four 16-byte unaligned vector stores, proving the target, alignment assumptions, and optimization level all permit efficient SSE codegen. However, the constant-size memset expansion follows a different lowering path that scalarizes the operation: it builds a repeated-byte pattern in integer registers using multiplication by 0x0101010101010101 and emits eight 8-byte stores. This strongly suggests the bug is not in front-end semantics or legality, but in the middle-end/built-in expansion or x86 backend strategy for inline memset of fixed size. The failure pattern indicates GCC's memset recognizer/expander and cost model are not selecting available vector store sequences for this size/value pattern, even though equivalent vector code is clearly profitable and already generated in the intrinsic case.
possible_causes: The x86 constant-size memset expander likely prefers a generic scalar integer expansion for 64-byte fills instead of invoking a target-specific SSE/vec store sequence when SSE2+ is available.

A defect may exist in the built-in/libcall expansion path for memset (e.g. expand_builtin_memset or related store_by_pieces/set_by_pieces logic), causing it to lose or never form vector modes for fixed-size stores with runtime fill values.
The target cost model or instruction selection heuristics for inline memset on x86 may undervalue unaligned 128-bit vector stores and therefore incorrectly choose multiple 64-bit scalar stores.

There may be a missed optimization in the byte-broadcast formation path: GCC recognizes how to broadcast a byte into an XMM register for explicit intrinsics, but the memset lowering path only knows the integer replicate-by-multiply idiom and never attempts vector splat generation.

The backend's move-by-pieces/store-merging logic may have a mode-selection bug that caps store width at word/doubleword granularity for memset expansions, instead of selecting TImode/V16QImode stores on SSE-capable targets.

A target hook or backend policy specific to x86 string/memory operation expansion may be failing to account for constant lengths like 64 bytes where four movups stores are a better inline strategy than eight movq stores.

There may be a missed canonicalization/optimization opportunity between memset built-in folding and later vectorization/combine passes, so the memset expansion happens too early into scalar RTL and prevents later SSE formation.
evidence: Both functions have the same memory effect: fill 64 bytes with the byte value loaded from s[-1]/dst[-1].
The explicit SIMD version compiles to movd/pshufb plus four movups stores, showing SSE codegen is legal and available for this exact pattern under -O3 -msse4.2.
The memset version is inlined rather than called, so the issue is in GCC's inline expansion strategy, not in libc selection.
The memset expansion constructs a repeated-byte pattern with 0x0101010101010101 using imulq/mulq/addq, which is characteristic of a scalar broadcast path rather than a vector path.
The generated stores for memset are eight movq stores at offsets 0..56, indicating scalarized piecewise emission instead of 16-byte vector stores.
Unknown alignment cannot fully explain the choice, because the intrinsic version already uses unaligned movups stores successfully.
The discrepancy appears only between two lowering paths for equivalent semantics: direct vector IR from intrinsics versus built-in memset expansion.
The bug report explicitly describes a code-generation quality regression/gap: constant-sized memset does not use SSE instructions even though equivalent hand-written SIMD does.

selected_files.reason: Most suspicious because the bad code path is inline expansion of builtin memset rather than explicit SIMD intrinsics. The report shows GCC recognizes memset and lowers it into a constant-size fill sequence, but chooses scalar byte-broadcast arithmetic plus eight movq stores. That points directly at builtin memset expansion logic such as expand_builtin_memset or nearby decision code that selects how fixed-size memset is emitted.

Highly relevant because generic piecewise memory set expansion lives here, including clear/store-by-pieces style machinery used by builtins expansion. The observed output looks like a generic scalar set-by-pieces strategy was chosen instead of wider vector stores, so mode-width selection or piece emission logic here is a strong candidate.

Likely involved through x86 target hooks, cost modeling, and string/memory-operation strategy decisions. Since SSE4.2 is available and unaligned movups is already used for the equivalent intrinsic form, an x86-specific policy or hook may be telling the generic expander to prefer scalar 64-bit stores for this memset case.

Directly suspicious because x86 string/memory operation algorithms and thresholds are described here. A poor algorithm choice for fixed-size memset of 64 bytes could easily originate from the backend stringop selection tables or definitions that fail to prefer SSE-based inline stores for this size.

Plausible x86 backend expansion site for lower-level memory operation emission and SSE-capable store formation. If the builtin/generic memset path delegates to x86-specific expansion helpers, this file is a natural place for missed generation of V16QI/TImode stores or byte-splat materialization in XMM registers.

Relevant because this bug may be driven by a cost-model mistake rather than legality. If tuning data undervalues unaligned 128-bit stores or overvalues the scalar replicate-and-store sequence, GCC could consistently choose the inferior non-SSE expansion for constant 64-byte memset.

Potentially involved as the generic RTL expansion layer that mediates between middle-end memset expansion and target patterns/optabs. If vector-capable store patterns exist but are not being queried or preferred during block/set expansion, the issue could stem from this selection layer.

Less likely than builtin expansion, but still plausible because the final scalar memset form resembles a widened store-merging style transformation. If the memset is first represented as smaller stores and this pass merges only up to 64-bit chunks instead of vector-width chunks, it could help explain why no SSE stores are formed.

gcc/builtins.cc.summary: Return true if NAME starts with __builtin_ or __sync_.

gcc/builtins.cc.signature: bool called_as_built_in (tree node)
gcc/builtins.cc.summary: Return true if NODE should be considered for inline expansion regardless of the optimization level. This means whenever a function is invoked with its "internal" name, which normally contains the prefix "__builtin".

gcc/builtins.cc.signature: bool get_object_alignment_2 (tree exp, unsigned int *alignp, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *bitposp, bool addr_p)
gcc/builtins.cc.summary: Compute values M and N such that M divides (address of EXP - N) and such that N < M. If these numbers can be determined, store M in alignp and N in BITPOSP and return true. Otherwise return false and store BITS_PER_UNIT to alignp and any bit-offset to *bitposp. Note that the address (and thus the alignment) computed here is based on the address to which a symbol resolves, whereas DECL_ALIGN is based on the address at which an object is actually located. These two addresses are not always the same. For example, on ARM targets, the address &foo of a Thumb function foo() has the lowest bit set, whereas foo() itself starts on an even address. If ADDR_P is true we are taking the address of the memory reference EXP and thus cannot rely on the access taking place.

gcc/builtins.cc.signature: bool get_object_alignment_1 (tree exp, unsigned int *alignp, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *bitposp)
gcc/builtins.cc.summary: For a memory reference expression EXP compute values M and N such that M divides (&EXP - N) and such that N < M. If these numbers can be determined, store M in alignp and N in *BITPOSP and return true. Otherwise return false and store BITS_PER_UNIT to *alignp and any bit-offset to *bitposp.

gcc/builtins.cc.signature: unsigned int get_object_alignment (tree exp)

gcc/builtins.cc.signature: bool get_pointer_alignment_1 (tree exp, unsigned int *alignp, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *bitposp)
gcc/builtins.cc.summary: For a pointer valued expression EXP compute values M and N such that M divides (EXP - N) and such that N < M. If EXP is not a pointer, false is returned too.

gcc/builtins.cc.signature: unsigned int get_pointer_alignment (tree exp)
gcc/builtins.cc.summary: Return the alignment in bits of EXP, a pointer valued expression. The alignment returned is, by default, the alignment of the thing that EXP points to. If it is not a POINTER_TYPE, 0 is returned. Otherwise, look at the expression to see if we can do better, i.e., if the expression is actually pointing at an object whose alignment is tighter.

gcc/builtins.cc.signature: tree c_strlen (tree arg, int only_value, c_strlen_data *data, unsigned eltsize)
gcc/builtins.cc.summary: Compute the length of a null-terminated character string or wide character string handling character sizes of 1, 2, and 4 bytes. TREE_STRING_LENGTH is not the right way because it evaluates to the size of the character array in bytes (as opposed to characters) and because it can contain a zero byte in the middle. ONLY_VALUE should be nonzero if the result is not going to be emitted into the instruction stream and zero if it is going to be expanded. E.g. with i++ ? "foo" : "bar", if ONLY_VALUE is nonzero, constant 3 is returned, otherwise NULL, since len = c_strlen (ARG, 1); if (len) expand_expr (len, ...); would not evaluate the side-effects. If ONLY_VALUE is two then we do not emit warnings about out-of-bound accesses. Note that this implies the result is not going to be emitted into the instruction stream. Additional information about the string accessed may be recorded in DATA. For example, if ARG references an unterminated string, then the declaration will be stored in the DECL field. If the length of the unterminated string can be determined, it'll be stored in the LEN field. Note this length could well be different than what a C strlen call would return. ELTSIZE is 1 for norm

The strategy is to issue one store_by_pieces for each power of two, from most to least significant, guarded by a test on whether there are at least that many bytes left to copy in LEN. ??? gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx emit_block_move_hints (rtx x, rtx y, rtx size, enum block_op_methods method, unsigned int expected_align, HOST_WIDE_INT expected_size, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT min_size, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT max_size, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT probable_max_size, bool bail_out_libcall, bool *is_move_done, bool might_overlap, unsigned ctz_size)

METHOD describes what kind of copy this is, and what mechanisms may be used. MIN_SIZE is the minimal size of block to move MAX_SIZE is the maximal size of block to move, if it cannot be represented in unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT, than it is mask of all ones. CTZ_SIZE is the trailing-zeros count of SIZE; even a nonconstant SIZE is known to be a multiple of 1<<CTZ_SIZE. Return the address of the new block, if memcpy is called and returns it, 0 otherwise.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx emit_block_cmp_hints (rtx x, rtx y, rtx len, tree len_type, rtx target, bool equality_only, by_pieces_constfn y_cfn, void *y_cfndata, unsigned ctz_len)

LEN_TYPE is the type of the expression that was used to calculate it, and CTZ_LEN is the known trailing-zeros count of LEN, so LEN must be a multiple of 1<<CTZ_LEN even if it's not constant. gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx emit_move_change_mode (machine_mode new_mode, machine_mode old_mode, rtx x, bool force)

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx_insn * emit_move_via_integer (machine_mode mode, rtx x, rtx y, bool force)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A subroutine of emit_move_insn_1. Generate a move from Y into X using an integer mode of the same size as MODE. Returns the instruction emitted, or NULL if such a move could not be generated.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx emit_move_resolve_push (machine_mode mode, rtx x)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A subroutine of emit_move_insn_1. X is a push_operand in MODE. Return an equivalent MEM that does not use an auto-increment.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx_insn * emit_move_complex_push (machine_mode mode, rtx x, rtx y)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A subroutine of emit_move_complex. Generate a move from Y into X. X is known to satisfy push_operand, and MODE is known to be complex. Returns the last instruction emitted.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx_insn * emit_move_complex_parts (rtx x, rtx y)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A subroutine of emit_move_complex. Perform the move from Y to X via two moves of the parts. Returns the last instruction emitted.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx_insn * emit_move_complex (machine_mode mode, rtx x, rtx y)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A subroutine of emit_move_insn_1. Generate a move from Y into X. MODE is known to be complex. Returns the last instruction emitted.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx_insn * emit_move_ccmode (machine_mode mode, rtx x, rtx y)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A subroutine of emit_move_insn_1. Generate a move from Y into X. MODE is known to be MODE_CC. Returns the last instruction emitted.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static bool undefined_operand_subword_p (const_rtx op, int i)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Return true if word I of OP lies entirely in the undefined bits of a paradoxical subreg.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx_insn * emit_move_multi_word (machine_mode mode, rtx x, rtx y)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A subroutine of emit_move_insn_1. Generate a move from Y into X. MODE is any multi-word or full-word mode that lacks a move_insn pattern. Note that you will get better code if you define such patterns, even if they must turn into multiple assembler instructions.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx_insn * emit_move_insn_1 (rtx x, rtx y)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Low level part of emit_move_insn. Called just like emit_move_insn, but assumes X and Y are basically valid.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx_insn * emit_move_insn (rtx x, rtx y)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Generate code to copy Y into X. Both Y and X must have the same mode, except that Y can be a constant with VOIDmode. This mode cannot be BLKmode; use emit_block_move for that. Return the last instruction emitted.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx_insn * gen_move_insn (rtx x, rtx y)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Generate the body of an instruction to copy Y into X. It may be a list of insns, if one insn isn't enough.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx_insn * compress_float_constant (rtx x, rtx y)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: If Y is representable exactly in a narrower mode, and the target can perform the extension directly from constant or memory, then emit the move as an extension.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx push_block (rtx size, poly_int64 extra, int below)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Push a block of length SIZE (perhaps variable) and return an rtx to address the beginning of the block. The value may be virtual_outgoing_args_rtx. EXTRA is the number of bytes of padding to push in addition to SIZE. BELOW nonzero means this padding comes at low addresses; otherwise, the padding comes at high addresses.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx mem_autoinc_base (rtx mem)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A utility routine that returns the base of an auto-inc memory, or NULL.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: poly_int64 find_args_size_adjust (rtx_insn *insn)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A utility routine used here, in reload, and in try_split. The insns after PREV up to and including LAST are known to adjust the stack, with a final value of END_ARGS_SIZE. Iterate backward from LAST placing notes as appropriate. PREV may be NULL, indicating the entire insn sequence prior to LAST should be scanned. The set of allowed stack pointer modifications is small: (1) One or more auto-inc style memory references (aka pushes), (2) One or more addition/subtraction with the SP as destination, (3) A single move insn with the SP as destination, (4) A call_pop insn, (5) Noreturn call insns if !ACCUMULATE_OUTGOING_ARGS. Insns in the sequence that do not modify the SP are ignored, except for noreturn calls. The return value is the amount of adjustment that can be trivially verified, via immediate operand or auto-inc. If the adjustment cannot be trivially extracted, the return value is HOST_WIDE_INT_MIN.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: poly_int64 fixup_args_size_notes (rtx_insn *prev, rtx_insn *last, poly_int64 end_args_size)
static void emit_single_push_insn_1 (machine_mode mode, rtx x, tree type)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Emit single push insn.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static void emit_single_push_insn (machine_mode mode, rtx x, tree type)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Emit and annotate a single push insn.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static int memory_load_overlap (rtx x, rtx y, HOST_WIDE_INT size)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: If reading SIZE bytes from X will end up reading from Y return the number of bytes that overlap. Return -1 if there is no overlap or -2 if we can't determine (for example when X and Y have different base registers).

gcc/expr.cc.signature: bool emit_push_insn (rtx x, machine_mode mode, tree type, rtx size, unsigned int align, int partial, rtx reg, poly_int64 extra, rtx args_addr, rtx args_so_far, int reg_parm_stack_space, rtx alignment_pad, bool sibcall_p)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Generate code to push X onto the stack, assuming it has mode MODE and type TYPE. MODE is redundant except when X is a CONST_INT (since they don't carry mode info). SIZE is an rtx for the size of data to be copied (in bytes), needed only if X is BLKmode. Return true if successful. May return false if asked to push a partial argument during a sibcall optimization (as specified by SIBCALL_P) and the incoming and outgoing pointers cannot be shown to not overlap. ALIGN (in bits) is maximum alignment we can assume. If PARTIAL and REG are both nonzero, then copy that many of the first bytes of X into registers starting with REG, and push the rest of X. The amount of space pushed is decreased by PARTIAL bytes. REG must be a hard register in this case. If REG is zero but PARTIAL is not, take any all others actions for an argument partially in registers, but do not actually load any registers. EXTRA is the amount in bytes of extra space to leave next to this arg. This is ignored if an argument block has already been allocated. On a machine that lacks real push insns, ARGS_ADDR is the address of the bottom of the argument block for this call. We use indexing off there to store the arg. On mac

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx get_subtarget (rtx x)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Return X if X can be used as a subtarget in a sequence of arithmetic operations.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static bool optimize_bitfield_assignment_op (poly_uint64 pbitsize, poly_uint64 pbitpos, poly_uint64 pbitregion_start, poly_uint64 pbitregion_end, machine_mode mode1, rtx str_rtx, tree to, tree src, bool reverse)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A subroutine of expand_assignment. Optimize FIELD op= VAL, where FIELD is a bitfield. Returns true if the optimization was successful, and there's nothing else to do.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: void get_bit_range (poly_uint64 *bitstart, poly_uint64 *bitend, tree exp, poly_int64 *bitpos, tree *offset)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: In the C++ memory model, consecutive bit fields in a structure are considered one memory location. Given a COMPONENT_REF EXP at position (BITPOS, OFFSET), this function returns the bit range of consecutive bits in which this COMPONENT_REF belongs. The values are returned in *BITSTART and *BITEND. *BITPOS and *OFFSET may be adjusted in the process. If the access does not need to be restricted, 0 is returned in both BITSTART and *BITEND.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: bool non_mem_decl_p (tree base)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Returns true if BASE is a DECL that does not reside in memory and has non-BLKmode. DECL_RTL must not be a MEM; if DECL_RTL was not set yet, return false.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: bool mem_ref_refers_to_non_mem_p (tree ref)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Returns true if REF refers to an object that does not reside in memory and has non-BLKmode.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: void expand_assignment (tree to, tree from, bool nontemporal)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Expand an assignment that stores the value of FROM into TO. If NONTEMPORAL is true, try generating a nontemporal store.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: bool emit_storent_insn (rtx to, rtx from)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Emits nontemporal store insn that moves FROM to TO. Returns true if this succeeded, false otherwise.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx string_cst_read_str (void *data, void *, HOST_WIDE_INT offset, fixed_size_mode mode)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Helper function for store_expr storing of STRING_CST.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx store_expr (tree exp, rtx target, int call_param_p, bool nontemporal, bool reverse)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Generate code for computing expression EXP, and storing the value into TARGET. If the mode is BLKmode then we may return TARGET itself. It turns out that in BLKmode it doesn't cause a problem. because C has no operators that could combine two different assignments into the same BLKmode object with different values with no sequence point. Will other languages need this to be more thorough? If CALL_PARAM_P is nonzero, this is a store into a call param on the stack, and block moves may need to be treated specially. If NONTEMPORAL is true, try using a nontemporal store instruction. If REVERSE is true, the store is to be done in reverse order.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static bool flexible_array_member_p (const_tree f, const_tree type)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Return true if field F of structure TYPE is a flexible array.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static HOST_WIDE_INT count_type_elements (const_tree type, bool for_ctor_p)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: If FOR_CTOR_P, return the number of top-level elements that a constructor must have in order for it to completely initialize a value of type TYPE. Return -1 if the number isn't known. If !FOR_CTOR_P, return an estimate of the number of scalars in TYPE.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static bool categorize_ctor_elements_1 (const_tree ctor, HOST_WIDE_INT *p_nz_elts, HOST_WIDE_INT *p_unique_nz_elts, HOST_WIDE_INT *p_init_elts, int *p_complete)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Helper for categorize_ctor_elements. Identical interface.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: bool categorize_ctor_elements (const_tree ctor, HOST_WIDE_INT *p_nz_elts, HOST_WIDE_INT *p_unique_nz_elts, HOST_WIDE_INT *p_init_elts, int *p_complete)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Examine CTOR to discover: how many scalar fields are set to nonzero values, and place it in *P_NZ_ELTS; the same, but counting RANGE_EXPRs as multiplier of 1 instead of high - low + 1 (this can be useful for callers to determine ctors that could be cheaply initialized with - perhaps nested - loops compared to copied from huge read-only data), and place it in *P_UNIQUE_NZ_ELTS; how many scalar fields in total are in CTOR, and place it in *P_ELT_COUNT. whether the constructor is complete -- in the sense that every meaningful byte is explicitly given a value -- and place it in *P_COMPLETE: - 0 if any field is missing - 1 if all fields are initialized, and there's no padding - -1 if all fields are initialized, but there's padding Return whether or not CTOR is a valid static constant initializer, the same as "initializer_constant_valid_p (CTOR, TREE_TYPE (CTOR)) != 0".

gcc/expr.cc.signature: bool immediate_const_ctor_p (const_tree ctor, unsigned int words)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Return true if constructor CTOR is simple enough to be materialized in an integer mode register. Limit the size to WORDS words, which is 1 by default.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: bool complete_ctor_at_level_p (const_tree type, HOST_WIDE_INT num_elts, const_tree last_type)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: TYPE is initialized by a constructor with NUM_ELTS elements, the last of which had type LAST_TYPE. Each element was itself a complete initializer, in the sense that every meaningful byte was explicitly given a value. Return true if the same is true for the constructor as a whole.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static bool mostly_zeros_p (const_tree exp)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Return true if EXP contains mostly (3/4) zeros.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static bool all_zeros_p (const_tree exp)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Return true if EXP contains all zeros.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static void store_constructor_field (rtx target, poly_uint64 bitsize, poly_int64 bitpos, poly_uint64 bitregion_start, poly_uint64 bitregion_end, machine_mode mode, tree exp, int cleared, alias_set_type alias_set, bool reverse)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Helper function for store_constructor. TARGET, BITSIZE, BITPOS, MODE, EXP are as for store_field. CLEARED is as for store_constructor. ALIAS_SET is the alias set to use for any stores. If REVERSE is true, the store is to be done in reverse order. This provides a recursive shortcut back to store_constructor when it isn't necessary to go through store_field. This is so that we can pass through the cleared field to let store_constructor know that we may not have to clear a substructure if the outer structure has already been cleared.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static int fields_length (const_tree type)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Returns the number of FIELD_DECLs in TYPE.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: void store_constructor (tree exp, rtx target, int cleared, poly_int64 size, bool reverse)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Store the value of constructor EXP into the rtx TARGET. TARGET is either a REG or a MEM; we know it cannot conflict, since safe_from_p has been called. CLEARED is true if TARGET is known to have been zero'd. SIZE is the number of bytes of TARGET we are allowed to modify: this may not be the same as the size of EXP if we are assigning to a field which has been packed to exclude padding bits. If REVERSE is true, the store is to be done in reverse order.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx store_field (rtx target, poly_int64 bitsize, poly_int64 bitpos, poly_uint64 bitregion_start, poly_uint64 bitregion_end, machine_mode mode, tree exp, alias_set_type alias_set, bool nontemporal, bool reverse)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Store the value of EXP (an expression tree) into a subfield of TARGET which has mode MODE and occupies BITSIZE bits, starting BITPOS bits from the start of TARGET. If MODE is VOIDmode, it means that we are storing into a bit-field. BITREGION_START is bitpos of the first bitfield in this region. BITREGION_END is the bitpos of the ending bitfield in this region. These two fields are 0, if the C++ memory model does not apply, or we are not interested in keeping track of bitfield regions. Always return const0_rtx unless we have something particular to return. ALIAS_SET is the alias set for the destination. This value will (in general) be different from that for TARGET, since TARGET is a reference to the containing structure. If NONTEMPORAL is true, try generating a nontemporal store. If REVERSE is true, the store is to be done in reverse order.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: tree get_inner_reference (tree exp, poly_int64 *pbitsize, poly_int64 *pbitpos, tree *poffset, machine_mode *pmode, int *punsignedp, int *preversep, int *pvolatilep)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Given an expression EXP that may be a COMPONENT_REF, a BIT_FIELD_REF, an ARRAY_REF, or an ARRAY_RANGE_REF, look for nested operations of these codes and find the ultimate containing object, which we return. We set *PBITSIZE to the size in bits that we want, *PBITPOS to the bit position, *PUNSIGNEDP to the signedness and *PREVERSEP to the storage order of the field. If the position of the field is variable, we store a tree giving the variable offset (in units) in *POFFSET. This offset is in addition to the bit position. If the position is not variable, we store 0 in *POFFSET. If any of the extraction expressions is volatile, we store 1 in *PVOLATILEP. Otherwise we don't change that. If the field is a non-BLKmode bit-field, *PMODE is set to VOIDmode. Otherwise, it is a mode that can be used to access the field. If the field describes a variable-sized object, *PMODE is set to BLKmode and *PBITSIZE is set to -1. An access cannot be made in this case, but the address of the object can be found.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT target_align (const_tree target)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Alignment in bits the TARGET of an assignment may be assumed to have.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx force_operand (rtx value, rtx target)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Given an rtx VALUE that may contain additions and multiplications, return an equivalent value that just refers to a register, memory, or constant. This is done by generating instructions to perform the arithmetic and returning a pseudo-register containing the value. The returned value may be a REG, SUBREG, MEM or constant.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: bool safe_from_p (const_rtx x, tree exp, int top_p)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Subroutine of expand_expr: return true iff there is no way that EXP can reference X, which is being modified. TOP_P is nonzero if this call is going to be used to determine whether we need a temporary for EXP, as opposed to a recursive call to this function. It is always safe for this routine to return false since it merely searches for optimization opportunities.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT highest_pow2_factor (const_tree exp)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Return the highest power of two that EXP is known to be a multiple of. This is used in updating alignment of MEMs in array references.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT highest_pow2_factor_for_target (const_tree target, const_tree exp)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Similar, except that the alignment requirements of TARGET are taken into account. Assume it is at least as aligned as its type, unless it is a COMPONENT_REF in which case the layout of the structure gives the alignment.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static enum rtx_code convert_tree_comp_to_rtx (enum tree_code tcode, int unsignedp)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Convert the tree comparison code TCODE to the rtl one where the signedness is UNSIGNEDP.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: void expand_operands (tree exp0, tree exp1, rtx target, rtx *op0, rtx *op1, enum expand_modifier modifier)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Subroutine of expand_expr. Expand the two operands of a binary expression EXP0 and EXP1 placing the results in OP0 and OP1. The value may be stored in TARGET if TARGET is nonzero. The MODIFIER argument is as documented by expand_expr.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx expand_expr_constant (tree exp, int defer, enum expand_modifier modifier)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Return a MEM that contains constant EXP. DEFER is as for output_constant_def and MODIFIER is as for expand_expr.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx expand_expr_addr_expr_1 (tree exp, rtx target, scalar_int_mode tmode, enum expand_modifier modifier, addr_space_t as)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A subroutine of expand_expr_addr_expr. Evaluate the address of EXP. The TARGET, TMODE and MODIFIER arguments are as for expand_expr.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx expand_expr_addr_expr (tree exp, rtx target, machine_mode tmode, enum expand_modifier modifier)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A subroutine of expand_expr. Evaluate EXP, which is an ADDR_EXPR. The TARGET, TMODE and MODIFIER arguments are as for expand_expr.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx expand_constructor (tree exp, rtx target, enum expand_modifier modifier, bool avoid_temp_mem)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Generate code for computing CONSTRUCTOR EXP. An rtx for the computed value is returned. If AVOID_TEMP_MEM is TRUE, instead of creating a temporary variable in memory NULL is returned and the caller needs to handle it differently.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx expand_expr_real (tree exp, rtx target, machine_mode tmode, enum expand_modifier modifier, rtx *alt_rtl, bool inner_reference_p)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: expand_expr: generate code for computing expression EXP. An rtx for the computed value is returned. The value is never null. In the case of a void EXP, const0_rtx is returned. The value may be stored in TARGET if TARGET is nonzero. TARGET is just a suggestion; callers must assume that the rtx returned may not be the same as TARGET. If TARGET is CONST0_RTX, it means that the value will be ignored. If TMODE is not VOIDmode, it suggests generating the result in mode TMODE. But this is done only when convenient. Otherwise, TMODE is ignored and the value generated in its natural mode. TMODE is just a suggestion; callers must assume that the rtx returned may not have mode TMODE. Note that TARGET may have neither TMODE nor MODE. In that case, it probably will not be used. If MODIFIER is EXPAND_SUM then when EXP is an addition we can return an rtx of the form (MULT (REG ...) (CONST_INT ...)) or a nest of (PLUS ...) and (MINUS ...) where the terms are products as above, or REG or MEM, or constant. Ordinarily in such cases we would output mul or add instructions and then return a pseudo reg containing the sum. EXPAND_INITIALIZER is much like EXPAND_SUM except that it also marks a label as ab

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx expand_cond_expr_using_cmove (tree treeop0 ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED, tree treeop1 ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED, tree treeop2 ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Try to expand the conditional expression which is represented by TREEOP0 ? TREEOP1 : TREEOP2 using conditonal moves. If it succeeds return the rtl reg which represents the result. Otherwise return NULL_RTX.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx expand_misaligned_mem_ref (rtx temp, machine_mode mode, int unsignedp, unsigned int align, rtx target, rtx *alt_rtl)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A helper function for expand_expr_real_2 to be used with a misaligned mem_ref TEMP. Assume an unsigned type if UNSIGNEDP is nonzero, with alignment ALIGN in bits. Store the value at TARGET if possible (if TARGET is nonzero). Regardless of TARGET, we return the rtx for where the value is placed. If the result can be stored at TARGET, and ALT_RTL is non-NULL, then *ALT_RTL is set to TARGET (before legitimziation).

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx expand_expr_divmod (tree_code code, machine_mode mode, tree treeop0, tree treeop1, rtx op0, rtx op1, rtx target, int unsignedp)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Helper function of expand_expr_2, expand a division or modulo. op0 and op1 should be already expanded treeop0 and treeop1, using expand_operands.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx expand_expr_real_2 (const_sepops ops, rtx target, machine_mode tmode, enum expand_modifier modifier)
static bool stmt_is_replaceable_p (gimple *stmt)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Return TRUE if expression STMT is suitable for replacement. Never consider memory loads as replaceable, because those don't ever lead into constant expressions.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx expand_expr_real_gassign (gassign *g, rtx target, machine_mode tmode, enum expand_modifier modifier, rtx *alt_rtl, bool inner_reference_p)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: A subroutine of expand_expr_real_1. Expand gimple assignment G, which is known to set an SSA_NAME result. The other arguments are as for expand_expr_real_1.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: rtx expand_expr_real_1 (tree exp, rtx target, machine_mode tmode, enum expand_modifier modifier, rtx *alt_rtl, bool inner_reference_p)
static rtx reduce_to_bit_field_precision (rtx exp, rtx target, tree type)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Subroutine of above: reduce EXP to the precision of TYPE (in the signedness of TYPE), possibly returning the result in TARGET. TYPE is known to be a partial integer type.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static bool is_aligning_offset (const_tree offset, const_tree exp)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Subroutine of above: returns true if OFFSET corresponds to an offset that when applied to the address of EXP produces an address known to be aligned more than BIGGEST_ALIGNMENT.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static tree constant_byte_string (tree arg, tree *ptr_offset, tree *mem_size, tree *decl, bool valrep = false)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Return a STRING_CST corresponding to ARG's constant initializer either if it's a string constant, or, when VALREP is set, any other constant, or null otherwise. On success, set *PTR_OFFSET to the (possibly non-constant) byte offset within the byte string that ARG is references. If nonnull set *MEM_SIZE to the size of the byte string. If nonnull, set *DECL to the constant declaration ARG refers to.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: tree string_constant (tree arg, tree *ptr_offset, tree *mem_size, tree *decl)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Return STRING_CST if an ARG corresponds to a string constant or zero if it doesn't. If we return nonzero, set *PTR_OFFSET to the (possibly non-constant) offset in bytes within the string that ARG is accessing. If MEM_SIZE is non-zero the storage size of the memory is returned. If DECL is non-zero the constant declaration is returned if available.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: tree byte_representation (tree arg, tree *ptr_offset, tree *mem_size, tree *decl)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Similar to string_constant, return a STRING_CST corresponding to the value representation of the first argument if it's a constant.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: enum tree_code maybe_optimize_pow2p_mod_cmp (enum tree_code code, tree *arg0, tree *arg1)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Optimize x % C1 == C2 for signed modulo if C1 is a power of two and C2 is non-zero and C3 ((1<<(prec-1)) | (C1 - 1)): for C2 > 0 to x & C3 == C2 for C2 < 0 to x & C3 == (C2 & C3).

gcc/expr.cc.signature: enum tree_code maybe_optimize_mod_cmp (enum tree_code code, tree *arg0, tree *arg1)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Attempt to optimize unsigned (X % C1) == C2 (or (X % C1) != C2). If C1 is odd to: (X - C2) * C3 <= C4 (or >), where C3 is modular multiplicative inverse of C1 and 1<<prec and C4 is ((1<<prec) - 1) / C1 or ((1<<prec) - 1) / C1 - 1 (the latter if C2 > ((1<<prec) - 1) % C1). If C1 is even, S = ctz (C1) and C2 is 0, use ((X * C3) r>> S) <= C4, where C3 is modular multiplicative inverse of C1>>S and 1<<prec and C4 is (((1<<prec) - 1) / (C1>>S)) >> S. For signed (X % C1) == 0 if C1 is odd to (all operations in it unsigned): (X * C3) + C4 <= 2 * C4, where C3 is modular multiplicative inverse of (unsigned) C1 and 1<<prec and C4 is ((1<<(prec - 1) - 1) / C1). If C1 is even, S = ctz(C1), use ((X * C3) + C4) r>> S <= (C4 >> (S - 1)) where C3 is modular multiplicative inverse of (unsigned)(C1>>S) and 1<<prec and C4 is ((1<<(prec - 1) - 1) / (C1>>S)) & (-1<<S). See the Hacker's Delight book, section 10-17.

Once expand_expr has been called on the arguments of the comparison, we are committed to doing the store flag, since it is not safe to re-evaluate the expression. gcc/expr.cc.signature: static void calculate_table_based_CRC (rtx *crc, const rtx &input_data, const rtx &polynomial, machine_mode data_mode)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Generate table-based CRC code for the given CRC, INPUT_DATA and the POLYNOMIAL (without leading 1). First, using POLYNOMIAL's value generates CRC table of 256 elements, then generates the assembly for the following code, where crc_bit_size and data_bit_size may be 8, 16, 32, 64, depending on CRC: for (int i = 0; i < data_bit_size / 8; i++) crc = (crc << 8) ^ crc_table[(crc >> (crc_bit_size - 8)) ^ (data >> (data_bit_size - (i + 1) * 8) & 0xFF))]; So to take values from the table, we need 8-bit data. If input data size is not 8, then first we extract upper 8 bits, then the other 8 bits, and so on.

This must generate a CRC table and an assembly for the following code, where crc_bit_size and data_bit_size may be 8, 16, 32, 64: uint_crc_bit_size_t crc_crc_bit_size (uint_crc_bit_size_t crc_init, uint_data_bit_size_t data, size_t size) { uint_crc_bit_size_t crc = crc_init; for (int i = 0; i < data_bit_size / 8; i++) crc = (crc << 8) ^ crc_table[(crc >> (crc_bit_size - 8)) ^ (data >> (data_bit_size - (i + 1) * 8) & 0xFF))]; return crc; }

Generate insns to zero all st registers together. Return true when zeroing instructions are generated. Assume the number of st registers that are zeroed is num_of_st, we will emit the following sequence to zero them together: fldz; \ fldz; \ ... fldz; \ fstp %%st(0); \ fstp %%st(0); \ ... fstp %%st(0); i.e., num_of_st fldz followed by num_of_st fstp to clear the stack mark stack slots empty. How to compute the num_of_st: There is no direct mapping from stack registers to hard register numbers. If one stack register needs to be cleared, we don't know where in the stack the value remains. So, if any stack register needs to be cleared, the whole stack should be cleared. However, x87 stack registers that hold the return value should be excluded. x87 returns in the top (two for complex values) register, so num_of_st should be 7/6 when x87 returns, otherwise it will be 8. return the value of num_of_st.

gcc/optabs.cc.signature: static bool add_equal_note (rtx_insn *insns, rtx target, enum rtx_code code, rtx op0, rtx op1, machine_mode op0_mode)
gcc/optabs.cc.summary: Add a REG_EQUAL note to the last insn in INSNS. TARGET is being set to the result of operation CODE applied to OP0 (and OP1 if it is a binary operation). OP0_MODE is OP0's mode. If the last insn does not set TARGET, don't do anything, but return true. If the last insn or a previous insn sets TARGET and TARGET is one of OP0 or OP1, don't add the REG_EQUAL note but return false. Our caller can then try again, ensuring that TARGET is not one of the operands.

gcc/optabs.cc.signature: static machine_mode widened_mode (machine_mode to_mode, rtx op0, rtx op1)
gcc/optabs.cc.summary: Given two input operands, OP0 and OP1, determine what the correct from_mode for a widening operation would be. In most cases this would be OP0, but if that's a constant it'll be VOIDmode, which isn't useful.

This routine must avoid generating such shifts for OP1s in the range [0, BITS_PER_WORD * 2). This function return NULL_RTX if anything goes wrong, in which case it may have already emitted instructions which need to be deleted. If we want to multiply two two-word values and have normal and widening multiplies of single-word values, we can do this with three smaller multiplications. The multiplication proceeds as follows: _______________________ [__op0_high_|__op0_low__] _______________________ [__op1_high_|__op1_low__] _______________________________________________ _______________________ (1) [__op0_low__*__op1_low__] _______________________ (2a) [__op0_low__*__op1_high_] _______________________ (2b) [__op0_high_*__op1_low__] _______________________ (3) [__op0_high_*__op1_high_] This gives a 4-word result. Since we are only interested in the lower 2 words, partial result (3) and the upper words of (2a) and (2b) don't need to be calculated. Hence (2a) and (2b) can be calculated using non-widening multiplication. (1), however, needs to be calculated with an unsigned widening multiplication. If this operation is

gcc/optabs.cc.signature: static rtx expand_doubleword_mod (machine_mode mode, rtx op0, rtx op1, bool unsignedp)
gcc/optabs.cc.summary: Subroutine of expand_binop. Optimize unsigned double-word OP0 % OP1 for constant OP1. If for some bit in [BITS_PER_WORD / 2, BITS_PER_WORD] range (prefer higher bits) ((1w << bit) % OP1) == 1, then the modulo can be computed in word-mode as ((OP0 & (bit - 1)) + ((OP0 >> bit) & (bit - 1)) + (OP0 >> (2 * bit))) % OP1. Whether we need to sum 2, 3 or 4 values depends on the bit value, if 2, then carry from the addition needs to be added too, i.e. like: sum += __builtin_add_overflow (low, high, &sum) Optimize signed double-word OP0 % OP1 similarly, just apply some correction factor to the sum before doing unsigned remainder, in the form of sum += (((signed) OP0 >> (2 * BITS_PER_WORD - 1)) & const); then perform unsigned remainder = sum % OP1; and finally remainder += ((signed) OP0 >> (2 * BITS_PER_WORD - 1)) & (1 - OP1);

gcc/optabs.cc.signature: rtx expand_doubleword_divmod (machine_mode mode, rtx op0, rtx op1, rtx *rem, bool unsignedp)
gcc/optabs.cc.summary: Similarly to the above function, but compute both quotient and remainder. Quotient can be computed from the remainder as: rem = op0 % op1; // Handled using expand_doubleword_mod quot = (op0 - rem) * inv; // inv is multiplicative inverse of op1 modulo 2 * BITS_PER_WORD We can also handle cases where op1 is a multiple of power of two constant and constant handled by expand_doubleword_mod. op11 = 1 << __builtin_ctz (op1); op12 = op1 / op11; rem1 = op0 % op12; // Handled using expand_doubleword_mod quot1 = (op0 - rem1) * inv; // inv is multiplicative inverse of op12 modulo 2 * BITS_PER_WORD rem = (quot1 % op11) * op12 + rem1; quot = quot1 / op11;

Either TARG0 or TARG1 may be zero, but what that means is that the result is not actually wanted. We will generate it into a dummy pseudo-reg and discard it. They may not both be zero. gcc/optabs.cc.signature: static rtx expand_ctz (scalar_int_mode mode, rtx op0, rtx target)
gcc/optabs.cc.summary: Try calculating ctz(x) as K - clz(x & -x) , where K is GET_MODE_PRECISION(mode) - 1. Both __builtin_ctz and __builtin_clz are undefined at zero, so we don't have to worry about what the hardware does in that case. (If the clz instruction produces the usual value at 0, which is K, the result of this code sequence will be -1; expand_ffs, below, relies on this. It might be nice to have it be K instead, for consistency with the (very few) processors that provide a ctz with a defined value, but that would take one more instruction, and it would be less convenient for expand_ffs anyway.

On success, return the instruction that performs the bit-test-and-branch and replace the second operand of *PTEST with the bit number to test. On failure, return CODE_FOR_nothing and leave *PTEST unchanged. Note that the comparison described by *PTEST should not be taken literally after a successful return. *PTEST is just a convenient place to store the two operands of the bit-and-test. VAL must contain the original tree expression for the first operand of *PTEST.

gcc/optabs.cc.signature: void emit_cmp_and_jump_insns (rtx x, rtx y, enum rtx_code comparison, rtx size, machine_mode mode, int unsignedp, tree val, rtx label, profile_probability prob)
gcc/optabs.cc.summary: Generate code to compare X with Y so that the condition codes are set and to jump to LABEL if the condition is true. If X is a constant and Y is not a constant, then the comparison is swapped to ensure that the comparison RTL has the canonical form. UNSIGNEDP nonzero says that X and Y are unsigned; this matters if they need to be widened. UNSIGNEDP is also used to select the proper branch condition code. If X and Y have mode BLKmode, then SIZE specifies the size of both X and Y. MODE is the mode of the inputs (in case they are const_int). COMPARISON is the rtl operator to compare with (EQ, NE, GT, etc.). It will be potentially converted into an unsigned variant based on UNSIGNEDP to select a proper jump instruction. PROB is the probability of jumping to LABEL. If the comparison is against zero then VAL contains the expression from which the non-zero RTL is derived.

Generate RTL for an asm statement with arguments. STRING is the instruction template. OUTPUTS is a list of output arguments (lvalues); INPUTS a list of inputs. Each output or input has an expression in the TREE_VALUE and a tree list in TREE_PURPOSE which in turn contains a constraint name in TREE_VALUE (or NULL_TREE) and a constraint string in TREE_PURPOSE. CLOBBERS is a list of STRING_CST nodes each naming a hard register that is clobbered by this insn. LABELS is a list of labels, and if LABELS is non-NULL, FALLTHRU_BB should be the fallthru basic block of the asm goto. Not all kinds of lvalue that may appear in OUTPUTS can be stored directly. Some elements of OUTPUTS may be replaced with trees representing temporary values. The caller should copy those temporary values to the originally specified lvalues. VOL nonzero means the insn is volatile; don't optimize it.
Emit code to jump to the address specified by the pointer expression EXP.
Generate RTL code for a `goto' statement with target label LABEL. LABEL should be a LABEL_DECL tree node that was or will later be defined with `expand_label'.
Output a return with no value.
Generate RTL to return from the current function, with no value. (That is, we do not do anything about returning any value.)
Generate RTL to return from the current function, with value VAL.
Generate RTL to evaluate the expression RETVAL and return it from the current function.
Expand a clobber of LHS. If LHS is stored it in a multi-part register, tell the rtl optimizers that its value is no longer needed.
A subroutine of expand_gimple_stmt, expanding one gimple statement STMT that doesn't require special handling for outgoing edges. That is no tailcalls and no GIMPLE_COND.

Expand one gimple statement STMT and return the last RTL instruction before any of the newly generated ones. In addition to generating the necessary RTL instructions this also sets REG_EH_REGION notes if necessary and sets the current source location for diagnostics.

Expand code to initialize the stack_protect_guard. This is invoked at the beginning of a function to be protected.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx * find_single_use_1 (rtx dest, rtx *loc)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: This is used by find_single_use to locate an rtx in LOC that contains exactly one use of DEST, which is typically a REG. It returns a pointer to the innermost rtx expression containing DEST. Appearances of DEST that are being used to totally replace it are not counted.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx * find_single_use (rtx dest, rtx_insn *insn, rtx_insn **ploc)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if DEST, produced in INSN, is used only a single time in the sequel. If so, return a pointer to the innermost rtx expression in which it is used. If PLOC is nonzero, *PLOC is set to the insn containing the single use. Otherwise, we find the single use by finding an insn that has a LOG_LINKS pointing at INSN and has a REG_DEAD note for DEST. If DEST is only referenced once in that insn, we know that it must be the first and last insn referencing DEST.

Because computing NEWVAL might also call SUBST, we have to compute it before we put anything into the undo table.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void do_SUBST_INT (int *into, int newval)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Similar to SUBST, but NEWVAL is an int expression. Note that substitution for the value of a HOST_WIDE_INT value (including CONST_INT) is not safe.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void do_SUBST_LINK (struct insn_link **into, struct insn_link *newval)

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool combine_validate_cost (rtx_insn *i0, rtx_insn *i1, rtx_insn *i2, rtx_insn *i3, rtx newpat, rtx newi2pat, rtx newotherpat)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Subroutine of try_combine. Determine whether the replacement patterns NEWPAT, NEWI2PAT and NEWOTHERPAT are more expensive according to insn_cost than the original sequence I0, I1, I2, I3 and undobuf.other_insn. Note that I0, I1 and/or NEWI2PAT may be NULL_RTX. Similarly, NEWOTHERPAT and undobuf.other_insn may also both be NULL_RTX. gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool delete_noop_moves (void)

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void setup_incoming_promotions (rtx_insn *first)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Set up any promoted values for incoming argument registers.

For 2.5, try to tighten up the MD files in this regard instead of this kludge.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void set_nonzero_bits_and_sign_copies (rtx x, const_rtx set, void *data)

If we are setting only a portion of X and we can't figure out what portion, assume all bits will be used since we don't know what will be happening. Similarly, set how many bits of X are known to be copies of the sign bit at all locations in the function. This is the smallest number implied by any set of X.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool can_combine_p (rtx_insn *insn, rtx_insn *i3, rtx_insn *pred ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED, rtx_insn *pred2 ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED, rtx_insn *succ, rtx_insn *succ2, rtx *pdest, rtx *psrc)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if INSN can be combined into I3. PRED, PRED2, SUCC and SUCC2 are optionally insns that were previously combined into I3 or that will be combined into the merger of INSN and I3. The order is PRED, PRED2, INSN, SUCC, SUCC2, I3. Return false if the combination is not allowed for any reason. If the combination is allowed, *PDEST will be set to the single destination of INSN and *PSRC to the single source, and this function will return true.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool combinable_i3pat (rtx_insn *i3, rtx *loc, rtx i2dest, rtx i1dest, rtx i0dest, bool i1_not_in_src, bool i0_not_in_src, rtx *pi3dest_killed)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: LOC is the location within I3 that contains its pattern or the component of a PARALLEL of the pattern. We validate that it is valid for combining. One problem is if I3 modifies its output, as opposed to replacing it entirely, we can't allow the output to contain I2DEST, I1DEST or I0DEST as doing so would produce an insn that is not equivalent to the original insns. Consider: (set (reg:DI 101) (reg:DI 100)) (set (subreg:SI (reg:DI 101) 0) <foo>) This is NOT equivalent to: (parallel [(set (subreg:SI (reg:DI 100) 0) <foo>) (set (reg:DI 101) (reg:DI 100))]) Not only does this modify 100 (in which case it might still be valid if 100 were dead in I2), it sets 101 to the ORIGINAL value of 100. We can also run into a problem if I2 sets a register that I1 uses and I1 gets directly substituted into I3 (not via I2). In that case, we would be getting the wrong value of I2DEST into I3, so we must reject the combination. This case occurs when I2 and I1 both feed into I3, rather than when I1 feeds into I2, which feeds into I3. If I1_NOT_IN_SRC is nonzero, it means that finding I1 in the source of a SET must prevent combination from occurring. The same situation can occur for I0, in which case I0_

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool contains_muldiv (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return true if X is an arithmetic expression that contains a multiplication and division. We don't count multiplications by powers of two here.

gcc/combine.cc.summary: Determine whether INSN can be used in a combination. Return true if not. This is used in try_combine to detect early some cases where we can't perform combinations.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool reg_subword_p (rtx x, rtx reg)

gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return whether PAT is a PARALLEL of exactly N register SETs followed by an arbitrary number of CLOBBERs.

gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return whether INSN, a PARALLEL of N register SETs (and maybe some CLOBBERs), can be split into individual SETs in that order, without changing semantics.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool is_just_move (rtx_insn *x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return whether X is just a single_set, with the source a general_operand.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int count_auto_inc (rtx, rtx, rtx, rtx, rtx, void *arg)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Callback function to count autoincs.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx_insn * try_combine (rtx_insn *i3, rtx_insn *i2, rtx_insn *i1, rtx_insn *i0, bool *new_direct_jump_p, rtx_insn *last_combined_insn)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Try to combine the insns I0, I1 and I2 into I3. Here I0, I1 and I2 appear earlier than I3. I0 and I1 can be zero; then we combine just I2 into I3, or I1 and I2 into I3. If we are combining more than two insns and the resulting insn is not recognized, try splitting it into two insns. If that happens, I2 and I3 are retained and I1/I0 are pseudo-deleted by turning them into a NOTE. Otherwise, I0, I1 and I2 are pseudo-deleted. Return 0 if the combination does not work. Then nothing is changed. If we did the combination, return the insn at which combine should resume scanning. Set NEW_DIRECT_JUMP_P to true if try_combine creates a new direct jump instruction. LAST_COMBINED_INSN is either I3, or some insn after I3 that has been I3 passed to an earlier try_combine within the same basic block.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void * get_undo_marker (void)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Get a marker for undoing to the current state.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void undo_to_marker (void *marker)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Undo the modifications up to the marker.

gcc/combine.cc.summary: Undo all the modifications recorded in undobuf.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void undo_commit (void)

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx * find_split_point (rtx *loc, rtx_insn *insn, bool set_src)

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx subst (rtx x, rtx from, rtx to, bool in_dest, bool in_cond, bool unique_copy)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Throughout X, replace FROM with TO, and return the result. The result is TO if X is FROM; otherwise the result is X, but its contents may have been modified. If they were modified, a record was made in undobuf so that undo_all will (among other things) return X to its original state. If the number of changes necessary is too much to record to undo, the excess changes are not made, so the result is invalid. The changes already made can still be undone. undobuf.num_undo is incremented for such changes, so by testing that the caller can tell whether the result is valid. `n_occurrences' is incremented each time FROM is replaced. IN_DEST is true if we are processing the SET_DEST of a SET. IN_COND is true if we are at the top level of a condition. UNIQUE_COPY is true if each substitution must be unique. We do this by copying if `n_occurrences' is nonzero.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void maybe_swap_commutative_operands (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: If X is a commutative operation whose operands are not in the canonical order, use substitutions to swap them.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx combine_simplify_rtx (rtx x, machine_mode op0_mode, bool in_dest, bool in_cond)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify X, a piece of RTL. We just operate on the expression at the outer level; call `subst' to simplify recursively. Return the new expression. OP0_MODE is the original mode of XEXP (x, 0). IN_DEST is true if we are inside a SET_DEST. IN_COND is true if we are at the top level of a condition.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_if_then_else (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify X, an IF_THEN_ELSE expression. Return the new expression.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_set (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify X, a SET expression. Return the new expression.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_logical (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify, X, and AND, IOR, or XOR operation, and return the simplified result.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx expand_compound_operation (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: We consider ZERO_EXTRACT, SIGN_EXTRACT, and SIGN_EXTEND as "compound operations" because they can be replaced with two more basic operations. ZERO_EXTEND is also considered "compound" because it can be replaced with an AND operation, which is simpler, though only one operation. The function expand_compound_operation is called with an rtx expression and will convert it to the appropriate shifts and AND operations, simplifying at each stage. The function make_compound_operation is called to convert an expression consisting of shifts and ANDs into the equivalent compound expression. It is the inverse of this function, loosely speaking.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static const_rtx expand_field_assignment (const_rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: X is a SET which contains an assignment of one object into a part of another (such as a bit-field assignment, STRICT_LOW_PART, or certain SUBREGS). If possible, convert it into a series of logical operations. We half-heartedly support variable positions, but do not at all support variable lengths.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx make_extraction (machine_mode mode, rtx inner, HOST_WIDE_INT pos, rtx pos_rtx, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT len, bool unsignedp, bool in_dest, bool in_compare)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return an RTX for a reference to LEN bits of INNER. If POS_RTX is nonzero, it is an RTX that represents the (variable) starting position; otherwise, POS is the (constant) starting bit position. Both are counted from the LSB. UNSIGNEDP is true for an unsigned reference and zero for a signed one. IN_DEST is true if this is a reference in the destination of a SET. This is used when a ZERO_ or SIGN_EXTRACT isn't needed. If nonzero, a STRICT_LOW_PART will be used, if zero, ZERO_EXTEND or SIGN_EXTEND will be used. IN_COMPARE is true if we are in a COMPARE. This means that a ZERO_EXTRACT should be built even for bits starting at bit 0. MODE is the desired mode of the result (if IN_DEST == 0). The result is an RTX for the extraction or NULL_RTX if the target can't handle it.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx extract_left_shift (scalar_int_mode mode, rtx x, int count)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if X (of mode MODE) contains an ASHIFT of COUNT or more bits that can be commuted with any other operations in X. Return X without that shift if so.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx make_compound_operation_int (scalar_int_mode mode, rtx *x_ptr, enum rtx_code in_code, enum rtx_code *next_code_ptr)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Subroutine of make_compound_operation. *X_PTR is the rtx at the current level of the expression and MODE is its mode. IN_CODE is as for make_compound_operation. *NEXT_CODE_PTR is the value of IN_CODE that should be used when recursing on operands of *X_PTR. There are two possible actions: - Return null. This tells the caller to recurse on *X_PTR with IN_CODE equal to *NEXT_CODE_PTR, after which *X_PTR holds the final value. - Return a new rtx, which the caller returns directly.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: rtx make_compound_operation (rtx x, enum rtx_code in_code)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Look at the expression rooted at X. Look for expressions equivalent to ZERO_EXTRACT, SIGN_EXTRACT, ZERO_EXTEND, SIGN_EXTEND. Form these expressions. Return the new rtx, usually just X. Also, for machines like the VAX that don't have logical shift insns, try to convert logical to arithmetic shift operations in cases where they are equivalent. This undoes the canonicalizations to logical shifts done elsewhere. We try, as much as possible, to re-use rtl expressions to save memory. IN_CODE says what kind of expression we are processing. Normally, it is SET. In a memory address it is MEM. When processing the arguments of a comparison or a COMPARE against zero, it is COMPARE, or EQ if more precisely it is an equality comparison against zero.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int get_pos_from_mask (unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT m, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *plen)

Return a possibly simplified expression, but always convert X to MODE. If X is a CONST_INT, AND the CONST_INT with MASK. gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx distribute_and_simplify_rtx (rtx x, int n)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if X is of the form (* (+ A B) C), and if so convert to (+ (* A C) (* B C)) and try to simplify. Most of the time, this results in no change. However, if some of the operands are the same or inverses of each other, simplifications will result. For example, (and (ior A B) (not B)) can occur as the result of expanding a bit field assignment. When we apply the distributive law to this, we get (ior (and (A (not B))) (and (B (not B)))), which then simplifies to (and (A (not B))). Note that no checks happen on the validity of applying the inverse distributive law. This is pointless since we can do it in the few places where this routine is called. N is the index of the term that is decomposed (the arithmetic operation, i.e. (+ A B) in the first example above). !N is the index of the term that is distributed, i.e. of C in the first example above.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_and_const_int_1 (scalar_int_mode mode, rtx varop, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT constop)

gcc/combine.cc.summary: We have X, a logical `and' of VAROP with the constant CONSTOP, to be done in MODE. Return an equivalent form, if different from X. Otherwise, return X. If X is zero, we are to always construct the equivalent form.

gcc/combine.cc.summary: Given a REG X of mode XMODE, compute which bits in X can be nonzero. We don't care about bits outside of those defined in MODE. We DO care about all the bits in MODE, even if XMODE is smaller than MODE. For most X this is simply GET_MODE_MASK (GET_MODE (MODE)), but if X is a shift, AND, or zero_extract, we can do better.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx reg_num_sign_bit_copies_for_combine (const_rtx x, scalar_int_mode xmode, scalar_int_mode mode, unsigned int *result)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Given a reg X of mode XMODE, return the number of bits at the high-order end of X that are known to be equal to the sign bit. X will be used in mode MODE; the returned value will always be between 1 and the number of bits in MODE.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: unsigned int extended_count (const_rtx x, machine_mode mode, bool unsignedp)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return the number of "extended" bits there are in X, when interpreted as a quantity in MODE whose signedness is indicated by UNSIGNEDP. For unsigned quantities, this is the number of high-order zero bits. For signed quantities, this is the number of copies of the sign bit minus 1. In both case, this function returns the number of "spare" bits. For example, if two quantities for which this function returns at least 1 are added, the addition is known not to overflow. This function will always return 0 unless called during combine, which implies that it must be called from a define_split.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool merge_outer_ops (enum rtx_code *pop0, HOST_WIDE_INT *pconst0, enum rtx_code op1, HOST_WIDE_INT const1, machine_mode mode, bool *pcomp_p)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: This function is called from `simplify_shift_const' to merge two outer operations. Specifically, we have already found that we need to perform operation *POP0 with constant *PCONST0 at the outermost position. We would now like to also perform OP1 with constant CONST1 (with *POP0 being done last). Return true if we can do the operation and update *POP0 and *PCONST0 with the resulting operation. *PCOMP_P is set to true if we would need to complement the innermost operand, otherwise it is unchanged. MODE is the mode in which the operation will be done. No bits outside the width of this mode matter. It is assumed that the width of this mode is smaller than or equal to HOST_BITS_PER_WIDE_INT. If *POP0 or OP1 are UNKNOWN, it means no operation is required. Only NEG, PLUS, IOR, XOR, and AND are supported. We may set *POP0 to SET if the proper result is simply *PCONST0. If the resulting operation cannot be expressed as one operation, we return false and do not change *POP0, *PCONST0, and *PCOMP_P.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static scalar_int_mode try_widen_shift_mode (enum rtx_code code, rtx op, int count, scalar_int_mode orig_mode, scalar_int_mode mode, enum rtx_code outer_code, HOST_WIDE_INT outer_const)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: A helper to simplify_shift_const_1 to determine the mode we can perform the shift in. The original shift operation CODE is performed on OP in ORIG_MODE. Return the wider mode MODE if we can perform the operation in that mode. Return ORIG_MODE otherwise. We can also assume that the result of the shift is subject to operation OUTER_CODE with operand OUTER_CONST.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_shift_const_1 (enum rtx_code code, machine_mode result_mode, rtx varop, int orig_count)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify a shift of VAROP by ORIG_COUNT bits. CODE says what kind of shift. The result of the shift is RESULT_MODE. Return NULL_RTX if we cannot simplify it. Otherwise, return a simplified value. The shift is normally computed in the widest mode we find in VAROP, as long as it isn't a different number of words than RESULT_MODE. Exceptions are ASHIFTRT and ROTATE, which are always done in their original mode.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_shift_const (rtx x, enum rtx_code code, machine_mode result_mode, rtx varop, int count)

If we cannot simplify it, return X or, if it is NULL, synthesize the expression with simplify_gen_binary. Otherwise, return a simplified value. The shift is normally computed in the widest mode we find in VAROP, as long as it isn't a different number of words than RESULT_MODE. Exceptions are ASHIFTRT and ROTATE, which are always done in their original mode.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int recog_for_combine_1 (rtx *pnewpat, rtx_insn *insn, rtx *pnotes, unsigned old_nregs, unsigned new_nregs)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: A subroutine of recog_for_combine. See there for arguments and return value.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool change_zero_ext (rtx pat)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Change every ZERO_EXTRACT and ZERO_EXTEND of a SUBREG that can be expressed as an AND and maybe an LSHIFTRT, to that formulation. Return whether anything was so changed.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int recog_for_combine (rtx *pnewpat, rtx_insn *insn, rtx *pnotes, unsigned int old_nregs, unsigned int new_nregs)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Like recog, but we receive the address of a pointer to a new pattern. We try to match the rtx that the pointer points to. If that fails, we may try to modify or replace the pattern, storing the replacement into the same pointer object. Modifications include deletion or addition of CLOBBERs. If the instruction will still not match, we change ZERO_EXTEND and ZERO_EXTRACT to the equivalent AND and perhaps LSHIFTRT patterns, and try with that (and undo if that fails). PNOTES is a pointer to a location where any REG_UNUSED notes added for the CLOBBERs are placed. If OLD_NREGS != NEW_NREGS, then PNOTES also includes REG_DEAD notes added. The value is the final insn code from the pattern ultimately matched, or -1.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx gen_lowpart_for_combine (machine_mode omode, rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Like gen_lowpart_general but for use by combine. In combine it is not possible to create any new pseudoregs. However, it is safe to create invalid memory addresses, because combine will try to recognize them and all they will do is make the combine attempt fail. If for some reason this cannot do its job, an rtx (clobber (const_int 0)) is returned. An insn containing that will not be recognized.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx gen_lowpart_for_combine_no_emit (machine_mode omode, rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Like gen_lowpart_for_combine but returns NULL_RTX for an error instead of CLOBBER. Note no_emit is not called directly from combine but rather from simplify_rtx and is expecting a NULL on failure rather than a CLOBBER.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static enum rtx_code simplify_compare_const (enum rtx_code code, machine_mode mode, rtx *pop0, rtx *pop1)

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static enum rtx_code simplify_comparison (enum rtx_code code, rtx *pop0, rtx *pop1)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify a comparison between *POP0 and *POP1 where CODE is the comparison code that will be tested. The result is a possibly different comparison code to use. *POP0 and POP1 may be updated. It is possible that we might detect that a comparison is either always true or always false. However, we do not perform general constant folding in combine, so this knowledge isn't useful. Such tautologies should have been detected earlier. Hence we ignore all such cases.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int count_rtxs (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Utility function for record_value_for_reg. Count number of rtxs in X.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void update_table_tick (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Utility function for following routine. Called when X is part of a value being stored into last_set_value. Sets last_set_table_tick for each register mentioned. Similar to mention_regs in cse.cc

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void record_value_for_reg (rtx reg, rtx_insn *insn, rtx value)
